The Torah Teaching and Historical Activity of Rabbi Dr. Judah Aryeh Leon Bibas: Herald of Active Zionism

This text surveys the revolutionary portrait of Rabbi Dr. Judah Aryeh Leon Bibas, an exceptional figure who combined profound Torah scholarship with broad academic and medical education. The writing emphasizes his contribution as central among the heralds of Zionism, as he called for abandoning passive expectation of a miracle and transitioning to active redemption including mass immigration, settlement, and even establishment of a Jewish military force. Through presentation of the stations of his life, from Gibraltar to Hebron, his decisive influence on his disciple Rabbi Alkalai is explained, and through him on the roots of Herzl's political Zionism. Finally, the article concludes with his personal story in the Land of Israel, focusing on the mystery of his lost library and the location of his historic grave in Hebron, which constitutes the closing of a circle for his national vision.

The Torah Teaching and Historical Activity of Rabbi Dr. Judah Aryeh Leon Bibas: Herald of Active Zionism

Introduction: The Intellectual Portrait of a Multi-Dimensional Leader

Rabbi Dr. Judah Aryeh Leon Bibas represents a pioneering and exceptional figure in the landscape of spiritual and public leadership of Jewry in the modern era.[1, 2] His activity exceeded the routine patterns of the rabbis of his generation, as he combined profound Torah scholarship as a halakhic decisor and kabbalist with broad academic education and a doctoral degree in medicine.[1, 2] His multicultural personality, his mastery of various European languages, and his numerous journeys among different Jewish communities in the Mediterranean basin and Western Europe shaped a unique cosmopolitanism.[1, 2] This involvement in the realities of the world enabled him to develop a broad-horizoned historical and political vision, by virtue of which he formulated one of the earliest and most daring national doctrines in the modern era.[1, 2]

The central contribution of Rabbi Bibas lies in his being one of the founding fathers of the proto-Zionist movement (heralds of Zionism).[1, 2] Decades before the appearance of the institutionalized political Zionism of Benjamin Ze'ev Herzl, Rabbi Bibas laid the ideological and practical foundations for the modern vision of the Return to Zion, while calling for abandoning the passive expectation of miraculous redemption and encouraging immediate transition to active undertaking, political settlement, and even military defense in the Land of Israel.[2, 3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Biographical Development and the Growth of National Consciousness

The geographical and intellectual trajectory of Rabbi Bibas is interwoven with the history of the communities of Spanish exiles in Western Europe and North Africa.[1] His wanderings and various life stations served as fertile ground for the growth of his national worldview, as they exposed him both to the distresses of exile and to the modern national struggles of the peoples of Europe.[1, 4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Theological Revolution: Transition from Passive Expectation to Active Redemption

The most significant contribution of Rabbi Bibas to Torah thought in the modern era lies in the paradigm shift in theology regarding the concept of "redemption."[2] In the nineteenth century, the overwhelming majority of the Torah world held a conservative and passive position, according to which one must wait for the coming of the Messiah with innocent faith and expectation of a supernatural divine miracle.[2] Rabbi Bibas challenged this conception and proposed a revolutionary interpretation of the sources.[2]

Redefining the Concept of Teshuvah

According to Rabbi Bibas's approach, the biblical and rabbinic concept of "teshuvah" – usually perceived as spiritual repentance, including fasts, mortifications, prayers, and weeping – requires practical transformation.[2] He argued that the term "teshuvah" derives its most direct literal meaning: physical and actual "return" of the people to their land.[2] The general and collective teshuvah required of the people of Israel prior to redemption is not an internal religious gathering in exile, but rather a physical, large-scale, and organized immigration to the Land of Israel and the establishment of permanent settlement there.[2, 4] These active deeds are the prior and sole condition through which it is possible to arouse the divine will and hasten the end of exile.[2]

Diagnosing Exile as National and Spiritual Illness

Rabbi Bibas did not view exile and the geographical dispersion of the people of Israel as a fate to which one must become accustomed, but rather as a severe pathological condition, which he defined as a physical and spiritual "illness" of the nation.[4] His thought presented a frontal and reasoned response to the motif of the 'Wandering Jew' – a prevalent Christian theological conception that claimed that the Jews were condemned to wander eternally without a homeland as punishment for rejecting Christianity.[4] Rabbi Bibas turned this bowl upside down; he explained that the dispersion and mass migration of the people among the lands are nothing but symptoms of the disease of exile, and the sole and absolute cure for this condition is national territorial concentration in the Land of Israel.[4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Geopolitical Inspiration and the Vision of Practical Liberation

The political conception of Rabbi Bibas was profoundly influenced by the dramatic historical processes that occurred in Europe and the Mediterranean basin during the nineteenth century. The period of his tenure as chief rabbi of Corfu brought him into close contact with the national struggle of the Balkan peoples.[1] The courageous stand of the Greeks and Serbs in rebellion against the rule of the Ottoman Empire, and their success in achieving political independence, served for him as tangible proof that national liberation does not occur on its own but requires sacrifice, organization, and practical struggle.[1]

From this geopolitical analysis, Rabbi Bibas proposed an idea that was unprecedented and particularly daring in the rabbinic world of his day: the establishment of a Jewish defensive military force.[3] He believed that the Jewish people must cease being subject to the mercies of the nations, display military resourcefulness, take up arms, and liberate the Land of Israel from Turkish rule by force of arms if necessary.[3] This vision of security and military sovereignty anticipated by decades the thought of the leaders of practical and political Zionism, and made him the definitive herald of the conception of Jewish self-defense in the modern era.[1, 3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Chain of Influence: From Gibraltar to Political Zionism

Although Rabbi Bibas did not leave behind many printed books, his halakhic and ideological system was transmitted to subsequent generations through his outstanding disciple, Rabbi Judah Alkalai.[1, 6] In 1831, upon Rabbi Bibas's appointment as rabbi of Corfu, the two met and Rabbi Bibas became the spiritual mentor of Alkalai, who then served as a young clergyman in Zemun, Serbia.[1, 6] Rabbi Alkalai adopted without reservation his teacher's revolutionary views concerning active redemption, pioneering immigration, and political organization, and began to disseminate them throughout Europe through his sermons and Torah compositions.[2, 6]

Through Rabbi Alkalai, a direct historical connection was created to the father of political Zionism, Benjamin Ze'ev Herzl.[3] Simon Loeb Herzl, grandfather of Benjamin Ze'ev Herzl, was an active member of Rabbi Alkalai's community in Zemun and was directly influenced by Alkalai's national teaching, which drew its sources from the doctrine of Rabbi Bibas.[3, 6] Thus Rabbi Bibas serves as the first and vital link in a chain of intellectual transmission that ultimately led to the establishment of the World Zionist movement.[3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Final Chapter in Hebron: Legacy, the Mystery of His Library, and the Location of His Grave

In 1852, a year after the death of his wife, Rabbi Bibas decided to translate theory into practice and end his life in the Holy Land.[1] Upon his arrival at the port of Jaffa, he was received with royal honor and great affection by his many disciples who awaited his coming.[1] From Jaffa he continued to the City of the Patriarchs, Hebron, where he chose to settle.[1,
In Hebron he established a significant Torah academy and housed within it his enormous and unique library that he had brought with him from Europe, a library that contained rare manuscripts and diverse books in the fields of Torah and science.[1]

His life in the Land of Israel was rather brief; only approximately two months after his immigration, on the 17th of Nisan 5612 (6 April 1852), Rabbi Bibas passed away.[1, 2] He was buried in the ancient Jewish cemetery of the Sephardic community in Hebron, in the section of holy ones designated for rabbis and kabbalists.[1, 5]

Historical Testimony and His Financial Estate

According to the historical records of James Finn, the British consul in the Land of Israel at that time, Rabbi Bibas left behind a financial estate of 2,000 piastres.[4] Half of the sum was given to the two faithful students who accompanied him on his final journey to the Land of Israel.[4] The second half of the money was dedicated, according to his will, to covering the expenses of his costly burial and to funding the performance of special prayers for the elevation of his soul each year during the Kol Nidre service on Yom Kippur eve in the synagogue of the Sephardic community in Hebron.[4]

The Mystery of the Rabbi's Library and the Connection to the Judean Desert Scrolls

During the Hebron massacre in 1929 (the events of 5689), the synagogues and Torah institutions of the Jewish community in the city were plundered, and Rabbi Bibas's magnificent library vanished as though it had never existed.[1] In 1953, the renowned scholar Professor Solomon Zeitlin advanced a revolutionary and controversial theory, according to which some of the hidden scrolls (the Judean Desert Scrolls) discovered in those years in the Qumran caves actually originated from Rabbi Bibas's private library that was plundered in 1929 and passed into the hands of local merchants.[1] Although this hypothesis remained a scholarly curiosity and did not achieve scientific consensus, it attests to the enormous reputation of the library as bearing rare and ancient spiritual treasures.[1]

Rediscovery of the Grave

For decades the precise location of Rabbi Bibas's burial in Hebron was unknown, following the extensive destruction wrought by the Jordanians in the ancient Jewish cemetery between the years 1948 and 1967.[1, 3] The growing historical and scholarly interest in his figure in recent years prompted meticulous search efforts and renewed examination of archival testimonies.[1, 3]

Solving the mystery was finally made possible thanks to the recollections of Yosef Ezra, a native of the city of Hebron, who provided precise topographical information that enabled identification of Rabbi Bibas's grave within the ancient section of rabbis and kabbalists in Hebron.[3, 5] The rediscovery of the grave constituted a closing of the historical circle for an eminent thinker who envisioned the revival of the people of Israel in their land, and who found his final resting place in the city of the Patriarchs.[5]
